statement: A ride has this sign: "You may not ride if you are under 12 years old or shorter than 140 cm." Of 30 children, 18 are under 12, 10 are shorter than 140 cm, and 7 are both. How many of the 30 may ride?

choices.misconception: I added 18 and 10 to get 28 children kept off, so I counted the 7 children who are both under 12 and short twice.
I used only the age rule and let in everyone who is 12 or older, forgetting the height rule.
I counted the children who are not allowed to ride instead of the ones who may ride.
I read "or" as "and", so I thought only the 7 children who are both under 12 and shorter than 140 cm are kept off.

hints: Is one broken rule enough to be kept off, or must a child break both?
The word "or" means one reason is enough. Count the children kept off without counting anyone twice, then take them away from 30.
Adding 18 and 10 counts the 7 children who are both twice, so $18 + 10 - 7 = 21$ children are kept off.

solutions.reliable: The word "or" in the sign means one reason is enough: a child is kept off if they are under 12, or shorter than 140 cm, or both. Adding $18 + 10 = 28$ counts the 7 children who are both twice, so the number kept off is $18 + 10 - 7 = 21$. The children who may ride are the ones who are neither under 12 nor shorter than 140 cm: $30 - 21 = 9$. The transferable idea: "not allowed if A or B" lets in only the people who are neither A nor B.
solutions.elegant: Set aside the 18 children under 12. That leaves 12 children, and of these $10 - 7 = 3$ are shorter than 140 cm. So $12 - 3 = 9$ children may ride.

whyOnTest: Kangaroo logic questions hinge on reading "or" and "not" exactly, and on counting an overlap only once.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
